name: Laxatives for weight loss

lead: Some people use over-the-counter laxatives to lower the number on the scale quickly and look flatter for a short time. The change is described as water-weight loss.

Laxatives act in the large intestine after nutrients have already been absorbed, so they mainly remove water and electrolytes rather than calories. A prospective study of 10,058 US women followed from 2001 to 2016 linked laxative and diet pill use for weight control to a later first eating-disorder diagnosis.

paras: People use it as a short-term scale-weight tactic, for example before a weigh-in or photo. Clinical literature classifies it as a purging behaviour associated with eating disorders, and eating-disorder services offer help.

Reported harms include dehydration, low blood pressure, electrolyte and acid-base disturbances that can be fatal, kidney damage and colonic problems. Laxative misuse is tied to anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa in clinical literature, and anyone struggling with it can seek support from an eating-disorder service.

chain: Flatter-looking stomach for a short time
angle.text: Some people take laxatives to drop scale weight and look flatter for a short time. The loss is mostly water rather than fat, and clinical literature classifies the behaviour as purging linked to eating disorders.

lead: Laxative use for weight control means taking laxatives not to treat constipation but to reduce body weight. [1][2] It is classified in clinical literature as a purging behaviour associated with eating disorders. [1][3]

Wikipedia notes that laxatives speed passage through the large intestine after nutrients are absorbed, so weight changes mainly reflect temporary fluid loss. [3] A prospective study of 10,058 US women followed from 2001 to 2016 examined diet pill and laxative use for weight control and subsequent first eating-disorder diagnosis. [1]
infobox: Non-medical laxative use for weight control

paras: Laxatives are grouped into bulk-forming, stool-softening, lubricant, hyperosmotic, saline and stimulant types, among others. [3] Wikipedia states that some people with anorexia or bulimia nervosa use them to lose weight. [3]
Because laxatives act after absorption, studies cited by Wikipedia find that weight changes mainly reflect temporary water loss, not calorie loss. [3]

Wikipedia lists dehydration (tremors, weakness, fainting, kidney damage), low blood pressure, rapid heart rate, severe hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis, rhabdomyolysis, colonic inflammation, pancreatitis and kidney failure, with electrolyte disturbances potentially fatal. Chronic stimulant use can cause melanosis coli, and the article describes concern that the colon may need increasing amounts to function, a point tagged as needing citation. [3]

sections.h: Associations with eating disorders and demographics
paras: In the longitudinal US study, diet pill and laxative use for weight control was examined as a predictor of a first eating-disorder diagnosis among young women. [1] A separate US cohort study of 13,683 adolescents and young adults found that laxative use for weight loss and muscle-building product use differ by gender and sexual orientation and examined childhood gender conformity as a contributing factor. [2]

The evidence is observational. The 2001-2016 cohort of US women and the 13,683-person cohort are described above. [1][2] A registered study examines inhibitory control in anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa and binge eating (n=17) and does not test laxatives directly. [4]
